summary: This document defines a placeholder X.509 signature algorithm for contexts where the consumer will not verify the signature. It updates RFC 5280.

eli5.summary: Sometimes a certificate form must have a signature box even though nobody checks it, so this gives a standard blank.

questions: what is an unsigned x509 certificate
why not use self-signed certificates as trust anchors
subtitle: A standard blank signature for X.509 certificates that carry subject information but have no real issuer.

tldr.problem: Some applications need only a certificate's subject information, such as a trust anchor, but X.509 has no unsigned form, so people attach self-signatures that nobody checks.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9925 defines the placeholder algorithm id-alg-unsigned, with an empty signature value, plus rules for filling in the issuer and extensions of such a certificate.
tldr.outcome: Receivers that verify signatures MUST reject it, so it can never pass as a real signature in a certification path. It also avoids large post-quantum self-signatures and key reuse.

today: RFC 9925 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2026. It updates RFC 5280 and has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Why Placeholder Signatures Cause Trouble
sections.content:
An X.509 certificate relates two entities: information about a subject and a proof from an issuer. Sometimes an application needs only the subject information, a node rather than an edge in the graph of the PKI. A trust anchor, which is trusted out-of-band, is one example.

X.509 has no structure for this, so trust anchors are often shown as self-signed certificates. Some TLS servers also use self-signed end entity certificates and expect the relying party to check them out-of-band, for example by a known fingerprint. These self-signatures typically have no security value and only meet syntactic requirements.

The RFC lists the drawbacks: post-quantum signatures are large, an end entity key risks cross-protocol attacks when it also signs X.509 data, it is unclear whether a self-signature requires the CA bit or keyCertSign, and a Key Encapsulation Mechanism (KEM) key has no valid signature algorithm at all.
sections.eli5: Making a fake signature nobody checks wastes space and can cause mix-ups. It is like writing a pretend autograph on a card just to fill the box.

sections.title: The Unsigned Signature Algorithm
sections.content:
To build an unsigned certificate, the sender MUST set both the Certificate's signatureAlgorithm and the TBSCertificate's signature field to an AlgorithmIdentifier with the algorithm id-alg-unsigned, which is {1 3 6 1 5 5 7 6 36}.

The parameters MUST be omitted, and the signatureValue MUST be a BIT STRING of length zero.
sections.eli5: You put a special 'unsigned' label in the signature box and leave the space empty.

sections.title: Filling In the Issuer
sections.content:
An unsigned certificate has no issuer, but the issuer field is not optional and both X.509 and RFC 5280 forbid empty issuers. Senders MAY therefore build the certificate as if it were self-signed when interoperability needs it.

If the subject is not empty, a sender MAY set the issuer to the subject. This is only a placeholder: the certificate is not considered self-signed or self-issued. Alternatively, a sender MAY use a short placeholder issuer: one relative distinguished name with one attribute of type id-rdna-unsigned ({1 3 6 1 5 5 7 25 1}) and a zero-length UTF8String value. In RFC 4514 string form that is 1.3.6.1.5.5.7.25.1=#0C00.

Senders MUST omit the issuerUniqueID field.
sections.eli5: The form wants an 'issued by' name, so you may copy the subject's name or write a special 'nobody' name.

sections.title: Extensions in an Unsigned Certificate
sections.content:
Two extensions describe the issuer and mean nothing here: authority key identifier and issuer alternative name. Senders SHOULD omit both. RFC 5280 normally requires the authority key identifier, with an exception for self-signed certificates used to distribute a public key; this document updates it to allow omission in unsigned certificates too.

The key usage and basic constraints extensions SHOULD reflect the subject. A CA subject SHOULD assert the keyCertSign bit and include basic constraints with cA set to TRUE. An end entity SHOULD NOT assert keyCertSign, and SHOULD omit basic constraints or set cA to FALSE, since the certificate does not issue itself.
sections.eli5: Skip the boxes about who issued it. Tick the boxes about what the owner is, such as a certificate authority or an ordinary user.

sections.title: Consuming Unsigned Certificates
sections.content:
A signature of type id-alg-unsigned is always invalid. A receiver that processes certificates without verifying signatures MAY accept it. A receiver that verifies X.509 signatures MUST reject it, and validators MUST NOT accept it in place of a signature in a certification path.

Most unmodified X.509 applications already comply. They are RECOMMENDED to simply treat id-alg-unsigned like any unrecognized signature algorithm, so the path fails at the signature verification step of RFC 5280.

Some applications may need changes. For example, one that checks self-signedness to classify configured certificates as trust anchors or untrusted intermediates may need to change its configuration model or user interface before using an unsigned certificate as a trust anchor.
sections.eli5: If someone has to check the signature, a blank one always fails. If nobody checks, a blank one is fine.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Limiting each key to one purpose is best practice. Self-signed end entity certificates force a key to be used twice, for the X.509 self-signature and for the end entity protocol. Unsigned certificates remove the self-signature and so fix this.

If an application accepted id-alg-unsigned where a signature must be verified, the check would be bypassed. The RFC compares non-compliant applications to those hit by the JWT alg:none problem.

An unsigned certificate also gives no integrity check, which some applications use with self-signatures against accidental storage corruption. They SHOULD use another mechanism, such as an externally verified hash.
sections.eli5: A blank signature must never be taken as proof of anything. Otherwise anyone could skip the check.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA has added three entries and one new registry. In the SMI Security for PKIX Module Identifier registry, decimal 122 is id-mod-algUnsigned-2025. In the Algorithms registry, 36 is id-alg-unsigned. In the SMI Security for PKIX registry, 25 is a new arc for Relative Distinguished Name Attributes.

That arc has its own registry, with 1 as id-rdna-unsigned. Future updates follow the Specification Required policy of RFC 8126.
sections.eli5: The official list of numbers got new lines so everyone uses the same codes for these labels.

items.text: A BIT STRING of length zero.
